reference.source: Grabb & Smith's Plastic Surgery / standard references
clinicalPearls: Orofacial clefts are among the most common congenital anomalies and may involve the lip only, the palate only, or both, and may be unilateral or bilateral, complete or incomplete
Cleft lip with or without cleft palate and isolated cleft palate are considered distinct entities with different embryology, epidemiology, and syndromic associations
A cleft may be an isolated finding or part of a syndrome, so a thorough assessment for other anomalies and genetic evaluation is important
Feeding difficulty is common with palatal clefts because the infant cannot generate adequate suction, and specialised bottles, teats, or feeding plates help maintain nutrition
Care is delivered by a multidisciplinary cleft team including surgery, orthodontics, speech and language therapy, audiology, ENT, genetics, and psychology
Lip repair and palate repair are staged over infancy, with palate closure timed to optimise speech development while balancing effects on facial growth
Cleft palate is associated with middle ear effusion and hearing loss from Eustachian tube dysfunction, requiring ongoing audiological monitoring

Long-term issues include speech and resonance problems (velopharyngeal insufficiency), dental and maxillary growth abnormalities, and the potential need for alveolar bone grafting and later orthognathic surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Orofacial clefting results from failure of fusion of the embryonic facial processes. Cleft lip arises from incomplete fusion of the medial nasal and maxillary processes, which normally unite to form the primary palate, during early facial development. Cleft palate results from failure of the palatal shelves to elevate, meet, and fuse in the midline to form the secondary palate. The aetiology is multifactorial, involving genetic susceptibility and environmental influences such as maternal smoking, alcohol, folate deficiency, and certain medications, and clefts can also occur as part of recognised syndromes.
additionalDifferentials: Submucous cleft palate (occult, with intact overlying mucosa)
Bifid uvula as a marker of possible submucous cleft
Pierre Robin sequence with cleft palate and airway compromise
Van der Woude and other syndromic clefts
additionalInvestigations: Prenatal ultrasound detection of cleft lip and counselling
Comprehensive newborn examination for associated anomalies
Genetic evaluation and karyotype or microarray when a syndrome is suspected
Audiological assessment and tympanometry for middle ear effusion
Speech and resonance assessment, including nasendoscopy or videofluoroscopy for velopharyngeal function
Dental and orthodontic evaluation and imaging before alveolar bone grafting
redFlags: Airway obstruction in Pierre Robin sequence or syndromic clefts, particularly with retrognathia
Failure to thrive from inadequate feeding and poor weight gain
Recurrent or persistent middle ear disease causing hearing loss and speech delay
Features suggesting an underlying syndrome with cardiac or other organ involvement
reference.prognosis: With coordinated multidisciplinary care most children achieve good functional and aesthetic outcomes, normal feeding, and intelligible speech, though some require secondary speech surgery, alveolar bone grafting, orthodontics, and orthognathic surgery into adolescence. Outcomes are influenced by cleft severity, associated syndromes, and access to specialist team care.
pitfalls: Missing a submucous cleft palate in a child with speech or feeding problems and a bifid uvula
Overlooking associated anomalies or an underlying syndrome
Underestimating feeding and airway difficulties in the neonatal period
Neglecting audiological follow-up, allowing undetected hearing loss to impair speech development
Timing palate repair without balancing speech benefit against effects on midface growth
management: Staged surgical correction, with lip repair in early infancy followed by palate closure timed to optimise speech development while limiting disturbance of facial growth.
Early feeding support using specialised bottles, teats or feeding plates to maintain nutrition where palatal clefting prevents adequate suction.
Speech and language therapy through childhood, with secondary surgery such as pharyngoplasty for velopharyngeal insufficiency where needed.
Audiological surveillance and ENT management of middle ear effusion, including ventilation tubes, to protect hearing.
Orthodontic care with alveolar bone grafting and later orthognathic surgery for maxillary hypoplasia and dental alignment.
Coordinated care by a multidisciplinary cleft team spanning surgery, orthodontics, speech therapy, audiology, ENT, genetics and psychology.
Genetic evaluation and family counselling where a syndromic cause is identified.
